params.question: A patient with bilateral progressive hearing loss has an audiogram showing conductive hearing loss with an air-bone gap and a characteristic dip at 2 kHz. Which condition does this pattern most likely indicate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A 4 kHz notch is the fingerprint of noise-induced hearing loss, not a 2 kHz dip. NIHL also produces sensorineural loss with no air-bone gap.
Correct. A conductive hearing loss with an air-bone gap and a dip at 2 kHz — Carhart's notch — is the audiometric signature of otosclerosis, caused by fixation of the stapes footplate.
Presbyacusis causes high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss without an air-bone gap. A 2 kHz notch with an air-bone gap points to a conductive cause — otosclerosis.
Acoustic neuroma produces unilateral sensorineural hearing loss without an air-bone gap. The 2 kHz conductive dip is Carhart's notch, characteristic of otosclerosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: This audiogram shows Carhart's notch at 2 kHz with an air-bone gap — the classic pattern of otosclerosis. Compare: a 4 kHz notch without an air-bone gap points to noise-induced hearing loss.
Carhart's notch at 2 kHz is a mechanical artifact of the fixed stapes in otosclerosis. It disappears after successful stapedotomy.

interactions.label: What explains paracusis Willisii, the paradox where a patient with otosclerosis

params.question: What explains paracusis Willisii, the paradox where a patient with otosclerosis hears better in noisy environments?

answers.text: The cochlea adapts more efficiently to louder sounds in otosclerosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The cochlea functions normally in otosclerosis — the pathology is stapes fixation, a purely mechanical problem. Cochlear adaptation does not explain this paradox.

answers.text: Background noise triggers a protective stapedial reflex that improves hearing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The stapedial reflex is actually absent in otosclerosis because the stapes is fixed. It cannot contract to improve hearing.

answers.text: Speakers raise their voices in noise, and the conductive loss filters out the background hum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In noisy settings, speakers naturally raise their voices. The patient's conductive loss attenuates the background hum, so the louder speech signal reaches the cochlea more clearly.

answers.text: Ambient vibrations bypass the fixed stapes through bone conduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While bone conduction bypasses the middle ear, random ambient vibrations do not selectively improve speech intelligibility. The mechanism is speakers raising their voices in noise.

overallFeedback.feedback: Paracusis Willisii has a simple two-part mechanism: speakers raise their voices in noise, and the conductive loss from stapes fixation attenuates the background hum, letting the louder speech through.
Paracusis Willisii occurs because a noisy environment prompts louder speech, while the conductive hearing loss simultaneously filters out background noise — giving a net advantage.

params.question: A patient presents with progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. What is the gold-standard investigation to confirm or exclude a vestibular schwannoma?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT demonstrates bony anatomy well but has poor sensitivity for soft-tissue tumours like schwannomas within the internal auditory canal.
ABR may show prolonged wave V latency, raising suspicion for a retrocochlear lesion, but it is a screening tool — not the definitive diagnostic investigation.

answers.text: MRI with gadolinium through the internal auditory canal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. MRI with gadolinium is the gold-standard investigation. Any unexplained unilateral SNHL mandates this imaging to exclude vestibular schwannoma.
Electrocochleography measures the SP/AP ratio and is used for diagnosing Meniere's disease (endolymphatic hydrops), not acoustic neuroma.

overallFeedback.feedback: The gold-standard investigation for suspected vestibular schwannoma is MRI with gadolinium through the internal auditory canal. The audiogram alone cannot exclude a tumour.
MRI with gadolinium is the gold standard for acoustic neuroma. Remember: bilateral tumours in a young patient raise suspicion for neurofibromatosis type 2.

interactions.label: A patient presents with episodic vertigo lasting two hours, fluctuating low-freq

params.question: A patient presents with episodic vertigo lasting two hours, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, and a low-pitched roaring tinnitus. Which additional feature completes the diagnostic tetrad of Meniere's disease?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nystagmus may occur during acute Meniere's attacks, but it is not one of the four diagnostic criteria. It is a sign of vestibular disturbance, not a defining feature.
Otorrhoea (ear discharge) indicates middle ear infection or cholesteatoma — not Meniere's disease. The fourth criterion is a pressure sensation in the affected ear.

Correct. The Meniere's tetrad comprises episodic vertigo (20 minutes to hours), fluctuating low-frequency SNHL, low-pitched roaring tinnitus, and aural fullness — a pressure sensation in the affected ear.
Headache with vertigo raises concern for vestibular migraine or posterior fossa pathology. It is not part of the Meniere's tetrad — the missing feature is aural fullness.

overallFeedback.feedback: The fourth criterion of the Meniere's tetrad is aural fullness — a sensation of pressure in the affected ear. It is the most commonly omitted feature in examinations.
Aural fullness is the most commonly omitted feature of the Meniere's tetrad. The underlying pathology is endolymphatic hydrops, confirmed by an elevated SP/AP ratio on electrocochleography.

interactions.label: Why does the 1-3-6 rule for managing childhood deafness emphasise fitting hearin

params.question: Why does the 1-3-6 rule for managing childhood deafness emphasise fitting hearing aids by six months of age?

answers.text: Cochlear implant surgery is technically safer before six months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cochlear implants are typically placed after 12 months of age. The urgency of the 1-3-6 rule is about neural plasticity, not surgical timing.

answers.text: The auditory cortex is most plastic in the first two years, and late identification causes lifelong language deficits

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The auditory cortex develops language pathways most actively during the first two years. A child implanted before 12–18 months can develop age-appropriate language; identification at four years leads to permanent deficits.

answers.text: Otoacoustic emissions become unreliable after six months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: OAE reliability does not decline with age. The 1-3-6 rule exists because early auditory input is essential during the critical period of cortical plasticity.

answers.text: Genetic testing for Connexin 26 must be completed before hearing aid fitting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Genetic testing is important for aetiology but is not a prerequisite for hearing aid fitting. The urgency is about the critical period of auditory cortex plasticity, not diagnostic sequencing.

overallFeedback.feedback: The 1-3-6 rule is driven by the biological critical period: the auditory cortex is most plastic in the first two years of life. Delayed intervention beyond this window causes lifelong language deficits.
The first two years represent the critical window for auditory cortex development. A child receiving amplification within this window has the best chance of age-appropriate language acquisition.
